# CATE product audit

## Feature Checklist

Each check marks implementation evidence in this checkout.

- [x] Project chat and attachments — `web/app/actions.js:133`
- [x] Send the same prompt to multiple models — `web/app/actions.js:137`
- [x] Review a plan before starting its steps — `web/app/actions.js:203`
- [x] Add model connections — `web/app/actions.js:291`
- [x] Choose a model for a task — `cate/core.py:109`
- [x] Gate dispatch on account availability — `cate/core.py:61`
- [x] Check cross-provider review eligibility — `cate/core.py:179`
- [x] Track run usage and limits — `cate/core.py:249`
- [x] Recover stalled work — `cate/core.py:268`
- [x] Restore browser drafts per project — `web/components/Chat.js:21`

## Bug Summary

Inspected 9 Python and 25 dashboard source files. Checks cover unresolved Python names and module imports, literal internal routes, interval cleanup and retained module caches. Findings need runtime verification.

- `web/lib/store.js:41` Module cache `cache` retains entries. Check whether the key set and retained values stay bounded.
- `web/lib/store.js:126` Module cache `mainCache` retains entries. Check whether the key set and retained values stay bounded.

### Conversation continuity

The worker prompt selects one project by chat ID and includes up to 24 recent messages (`cate/cli.py`, `conversation`). Instructions in another project or earlier in a long conversation can drop out of this handoff. Try a saved, user-editable project brief and check whether a second worker can recall a preference from it.
The dashboard supervisor receives up to 30 messages from the active chat (`web/lib/supervisor.js`, `history`). Reopening a saved chat and carrying context into a new project are separate behaviors to test.

## Competitor Analysis

These fixed examples use named 2024 model releases so the vendor measurements have a clear baseline. The reusable-context examples come from separate product documentation.

### OpenAI ChatGPT · GPT-4o

GPT-4o processes speech, images and text in one neural network. A person can ask about a photo in chat, a shorter interaction than submitting an attachment and waiting for a CATE worker. OpenAI reported a 320 ms average response to audio input, a model-level figure. ChatGPT Projects also lets related chats reuse project files and instructions. [GPT-4o launch](https://openai.com/index/hello-gpt-4o/) · [ChatGPT Projects](https://help.openai.com/en/articles/10169521-projects-in-chatgpt)

### Google Gemini Advanced · Gemini 1.5 Pro

Gemini uses a mixture of experts inside the model. CATE selects entire models for individual tasks. Gemini Advanced lets a user attach files from Drive or a device and ask about them together. Google reported 99% retrieval of a planted fact in its test with inputs up to one million tokens. That test measures recall within one input. For continuity across chats, a user can save instructions and reference files in a Gem. [Model and evaluation](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/products/google-gemini-next-generation-model-february-2024/) · [Gemini Advanced workflow](https://blog.google/products-and-platforms/products/gemini/google-gemini-update-may-2024/) · [Reusable Gems](https://support.google.com/gemini/answer/15146780?hl=en)

### Anthropic Claude · Claude 3.5 Sonnet

Claude pairs a hosted vision-and-text model with Artifacts, a pane for inspecting and revising generated work alongside the chat. A user can check the result while discussing it. Anthropic reported twice the speed of Claude 3 Opus and stronger results on its vision evaluations. CATE adds a different quality check by sending completed work to a separate reviewer. [Sonnet and Artifacts](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-3-5-sonnet)

### What to measure in CATE

Run the same document question and revision through direct chat and a reviewed CATE task. Record time to first answer, time to accepted result, charges or subscription tokens, and errors caught by review. A second chat with the same project instructions tests continuity. Use a non-secret preference for the recall test. These vendor measurements cover different tasks and cannot establish a CATE performance ranking.

It covers syntax errors, missing relative imports, unresolved names, dead routes (with dynamic routes, redirect aliases and public files allowed), interval cleanup and Map caches. It also confirms that `data/` is not scanned.

- The scan only reads source. It uses `ast`/`symtable` and never imports or runs the code it scans.

result.text:
# T0016: Architecture for a browser open-world crime/driving game

Author: claude-2. Status: architecture plan. No code is in this task; code starts in T0019.

## 0. Scope, constraints and one content rule

**The user asked for:** a "GTA Vice City" game that runs in the browser, built from scratch, as realistic as possible, and good enough to play through once.

**Content rule, which every later task must follow:** we build an **original game in the same genre**. That means a third-person open-world city where you walk, drive, steal cars, get a wanted level and play missions, set in a sunny 1980s-style coastal city. We do **not** copy Rockstar's names, map layout, characters, story, music, logos, vehicle designs or UI art. The working title is **"Neon Coast"** and the city is fictional. All assets are generated by us (procedural or hand-written code), which also fits the user's "make it from scratch". Reviewers should fail any task that imports ripped assets or trademarked names.

**Target and constraints**

| Item | Decision |
|---|---|
| Platform | Desktop browser: current Chrome, Edge and Firefox. Safari is best-effort. No install. Runs with `npm run dev` or as a static build. |
| Input | Keyboard and mouse (pointer lock) first. Gamepad (Gamepad API) second. No touch in v1. |
| Performance target | 60 fps at 1080p on a mid-range laptop GPU, with a playable 30 fps floor on integrated graphics through a "Low" preset. These are targets to measure against, not promises. |
| Size target | First playable load under about 30 MB, since most content is procedural. |
| Persistence | Single player. Saves go to `localStorage`/IndexedDB. No server. |
| "Realistic" means | PBR materials, shadows, a day/night cycle with sky and fog, believable car handling (raycast suspension and tyre friction), traffic and pedestrians that follow roads, collision damage and sound. It does **not** mean photoreal scanned assets, which are impossible from scratch in this effort. |

## 1. Tech stack, with the reasons

| Layer | Choice | Why this choice | Alternatives we rejected, and why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Language | **TypeScript** (`strict: true`) | Several different AI models will write modules separately. Typed interfaces at module boundaries catch integration mistakes at build time instead of at runtime. | Plain JS: too easy for agents to break each other's contracts. |
| Build/dev server | **Vite** | Starts with no config, has fast HMR, supports WASM and workers (`?worker`) natively, and outputs a static `dist/` that can be opened locally or hosted on GitHub Pages. | Webpack: slower and more config. Parcel: less common in three.js examples. |
| Rendering | **Three.js** (`WebGLRenderer` by default) | Largest WebGL ecosystem and documentation, which makes agents less likely to hallucinate APIs. It has the pieces we need: glTF/KTX2/Draco loaders, `InstancedMesh`/`BatchedMesh` for thousands of buildings and props, `LOD`, shadow maps, a Sky shader, and post-processing. MIT licence. | Babylon.js and PlayCanvas are strong all-in-one engines. **T0017 benchmarks them formally.** We default to Three.js so T0019 is not blocked, and this document limits engine-specific code to `src/render/` so a switch would stay contained. |
| Renderer backend | WebGL2 now. `WebGPURenderer` (`three/webgpu`) is optional later behind a flag. | WebGL2 runs everywhere. Three.js is actively improving WebGPU, but community reports in 2026 still show CPU overhead regressions in scenes with many meshes, which describes a city. Revisit after v1. | — |
| Physics | **Rapier** (`@dimforge/rapier3d-compat`) | Rust compiled to WASM: fast and deterministic. It ships official TypeScript typings. It has the two controllers this genre needs built in: **`DynamicRayCastVehicleController`** (raycast wheels with suspension, engine force, brake, steering and friction slip) and **`KinematicCharacterController`** (walking with slopes and steps). Normal JS objects, so no manual `Ammo.destroy()` memory management. The `-compat` build embeds the WASM, so no bundler WASM setup is needed. Apache-2.0. | **Ammo.js** (Bullet port, suggested in the brief): `btRaycastVehicle` is proven, but the API is C++-shaped, objects must be freed by hand (leaks are common), typings are unofficial, and builds are hard to obtain and update. Kept as **fallback only**: the `PhysicsAPI` boundary in §4 allows a swap. **cannon-es**: pure JS and easy, but slower with hundreds of bodies (traffic and props). |
| Audio | **Web Audio API** directly, wrapped in our own `AudioAPI`. Three.js `AudioListener`/`PositionalAudio` handle 3D positioning. | "From scratch" means engine, siren, horn, gunshot and ambience sounds are **synthesised** (oscillators, noise and filters) or generated offline by scripts. Web Audio does this natively. | Howler.js: built for file playback, not synthesis. |
| UI / HUD | **Plain DOM + CSS overlay** for HUD and menus. A **2D `<canvas>`** for the minimap and full map, drawn from the road graph. | Text, menus and layout are trivial in DOM. The minimap is a top-down vector draw of data we already have. No framework, so no extra bundle size or render loop. | React/Vue: overkill for about 10 widgets and adds a second update loop. In-scene 3D UI: harder to make sharp and readable. |
| ECS / game objects | A small **hand-written entity/component/system layer** in `src/core/ecs/` (about 200 lines): numeric entity ids, typed component stores and ordered systems. | Gives every agent the same pattern ("write a system that reads components X and Y"), keeps update order explicit, and avoids learning a library. | bitECS: fast, but its struct-of-arrays style is awkward for agents to write correctly. Deep class inheritance: tangles vehicles, peds and police together. |
| Maths | `three` maths types (`Vector3`, `Quaternion`, `Matrix4`) used everywhere | One maths library avoids conversions. Only render code touches the scene graph (§4 rules). | gl-matrix: a second maths library to convert between. |
| Assets | **glTF 2.0 binary (`.glb`)**, meshopt or Draco compression, **KTX2** (Basis) textures | The web standard. Three.js loads it natively. Exportable from code with `GLTFExporter` in Node scripts. **T0018 owns the details.** | FBX/OBJ: no PBR or compression, and slow to parse. |
| Tests | **Vitest** for pure logic (road graph, AI, wanted level, missions, physics adapter run headless with Rapier in Node). **Playwright** for one smoke test: the page boots, a canvas renders, no console errors. | "No errors" was an explicit user demand, so CI must prove the game boots. | — |
| Lint/format | ESLint (with `import/no-restricted-paths` to enforce §4 boundaries) and Prettier | Module boundaries are enforced by tooling, not by trust. | — |

**Dependency list for T0019:** `three`, `@dimforge/rapier3d-compat`. Dev dependencies: `typescript`, `vite`, `vitest`, `@playwright/test`, `eslint`, `prettier`, `@types/three`. Nothing else at runtime without a written reason in the PR.

**Where the code lives:** CATE agents work through PRs on this repo (AGENTS.md rule 7). The game should go in a top-level **`game/`** directory with its own `package.json`, merged through PRs from `cate/<task>-...` branches. A long-lived `browser-gta` branch, as T0019 suggests, would never be reviewed or merged under rule 7, so T0019 should use `game/` instead.

## 2. Architecture overview

```
                         +--------------------------------------------+
                         |                  main.ts                   |
                         |  boot -> load -> Game.start() -> loop      |
                         +---------------------+----------------------+
                                               |
     +-----------------------------------------v--------------------------------------+
     |                              CORE  (src/core)                                  |
     |  GameLoop (fixed 60 Hz sim + variable render)  ·  ECS World  ·  EventBus        |
     |  Clock/Time-of-day  ·  Config/Settings  ·  Services registry  ·  Logger         |
     +------+-----------+-----------+-----------+-----------+-----------+-------------+
            |           |           |           |           |           |
     +------v---+ +-----v----+ +----v-----+ +---v------+ +--v-------+ +-v----------+
     | INPUT    | | PHYSICS  | | RENDER   | | AUDIO    | | ASSETS   | | UI / HUD   |
     | kbd/mouse| | Rapier   | | Three.js | | WebAudio | | loaders, | | DOM + 2D   |
     | gamepad  | | adapter  | | scene,   | | synth,   | | cache,   | | canvas     |
     | -> Actions| | (only   | | camera,  | | 3D mix   | | procgen  | | (reads     |
     |          | | importer)| | lighting | |          | | registry | |  events)   |
     +------+---+ +-----+----+ +----+-----+ +----+-----+ +----+-----+ +-----+------+
            |           |           |            |            |             |
     +------v-----------v-----------v------------v------------v-------------v------+
     |                          GAMEPLAY  (src/game)                                |
     |  world/      city generator, road graph, chunk streaming, zones             |
     |  player/     on-foot controller, enter/exit vehicle, health, inventory      |
     |  vehicles/   vehicle defs, drive controller, damage, lights                 |
     |  camera/     follow-cam on foot / in car, collision, aim mode               |
     |  ai/         traffic drivers, pedestrians, police, pathfinding on graph     |
     |  combat/     weapons, hitscan via physics raycast, damage                   |
     |  wanted/     crime events -> heat -> police dispatch                         |
     |  missions/   data-driven mission scripts, objectives, triggers              |
     |  save/       serialize/restore                                              |
     +-----------------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

Dependencies only point **downward**. Core does not import gameplay. Gameplay systems talk to each other through **components** (shared data) and **events**, never by importing each other's internals.

## 3. Components

Each component lists its responsibility, the public API it exposes, and the task that owns it.

### 3.1 Engine core (`src/core/`), owned by T0019
- **GameLoop**: a fixed-timestep simulation at 60 Hz (`dt = 1/60`, at most 5 substeps per frame to avoid a spiral of death) and render once per `requestAnimationFrame` with interpolation `alpha` between the last two physics states. It pauses when the tab is hidden.
- **ECS World**: `createEntity()`, `destroyEntity(id)`, `add(id, Component, data)`, `get(id, Component)`, `query(A, B, …)`, and `addSystem(system, phase)`. The phases are `input → preSim → physics → postSim → ai → gameplay → camera → render → ui`.
- **EventBus**: typed pub/sub `on<E>(type, fn)` / `emit<E>(type, payload)`. Events are queued and flushed once per sim tick, so they never fire re-entrantly mid-physics.
- **Services**: one `Services` object passed to every system (`physics`, `render`, `audio`, `input`, `assets`, `events`, `settings`, `time`). No global singletons, which keeps tests easy to mock.
- **Settings**: quality presets (Low/Medium/High), key bindings and volume, persisted to `localStorage`.
- **TimeOfDay**: a game clock (1 real minute = 1 game hour by default) that drives lighting, traffic density and shop/street-light state.

### 3.2 Rendering (`src/render/`), owned by T0019 (base) and T0022 (city)
- `Renderer`: wraps `WebGLRenderer`, handles resize and pixel-ratio cap, tone mapping (ACES), sRGB output, and quality presets.
- `SceneManager`: the root scene plus layers for static world, dynamic entities and debug.
- `Lighting`: a sun `DirectionalLight` with **cascaded shadow maps** (three's CSM addon) or a single shadow camera that follows the player on Low; a hemisphere/ambient light; `Sky` and fog colour driven by TimeOfDay; and emissive street lights and windows at night.
- `MaterialLibrary`: a shared set of PBR materials (asphalt, concrete, glass, car paint, palm, sand, water) so draw calls batch well.
- `Instancing`: helpers that turn repeated props (palms, lamps, windows, parked cars) into `InstancedMesh`/`BatchedMesh`.
- `LOD and culling`: per-chunk LOD (high-detail meshes up to about 150 m, then merged low-poly blocks, then impostors or nothing beyond fog distance) plus frustum culling.
- `Water`: an ocean plane with three's `Water` shader for the coast.
- `PostFX` (High preset only): bloom for neon signs, SMAA, mild colour grading for the 80s look.
- `ViewSync` system (render phase): copies the interpolated physics transform into each entity's `Object3D`.
- `DebugDraw`: physics collider wireframes and road-graph lines, toggled with F3.

### 3.3 Physics (`src/physics/`), owned by T0020 (vehicle) and T0021 (character)
- `RapierPhysics implements PhysicsAPI`: **the only file group that imports Rapier.**
- Rigid bodies and colliders: static trimesh or compound boxes for buildings (built per chunk and removed when a chunk unloads), and dynamic boxes/convex hulls for props and cars.
- **Vehicles**: `DynamicRayCastVehicleController` (created with `world.createVehicleController(chassis)`; T0020 checks the exact call against the installed version). Four wheels, each with suspension stiffness, damping, rest length, friction slip and side stiffness. Engine force goes to the driven wheels and brake force to all.
- **Characters**: `KinematicCharacterController` with a capsule collider, autostep and slope limit, gravity applied by us, and snap-to-ground.
- Queries: `raycast`, `shapeCast`, `overlapSphere`, used by weapons, camera collision, AI sensors and interaction prompts.
- Collision groups: `WORLD_STATIC, VEHICLE, CHARACTER, PROP, PROJECTILE, SENSOR, CAMERA_IGNORE`.
- Contact events go to the EventBus as `collision` with impulse magnitude, which drives damage, sounds and crime detection.
- Option for later: move the Rapier world into a Web Worker. The `PhysicsAPI` is already async-safe in shape (commands in, transforms out), so this would not change callers.

### 3.4 World and city (`src/game/world/`), owned by T0022, with assets from T0018
- `CityGenerator` (pure, seeded): coastline and island masks, then **road network** (arterial grid with distortion, plus local streets subdivided by an L-system or recursive block split, a coastal boulevard and bridges between islands), then city blocks, then lots, then building footprints with height by district.
- Districts: beach strip with hotels, downtown towers, residential, docks/industrial and airport. All names are invented.
- **RoadGraph**: the single source of truth for roads. Nodes are intersections. Edges carry lanes, width, speed limit and direction. It is used by city meshing, traffic AI, pedestrians (sidewalks are offset edges), the minimap and mission GPS routing (A*).
- **ChunkStreamer**: the world is split into 256 m × 256 m chunks. Chunks within radius R are loaded (mesh, colliders and parked cars), and far chunks are unloaded with their resources freed. Generation is seeded, so a chunk regenerates identically.
- `Zones`: named areas used for the HUD "entered zone" banner, police response and ped/car spawn tables.
- Output contract: `generateCity(seed, params) → CityData { roadGraph, blocks, buildings, props, spawnPoints, zones, bounds }`, which is plain JSON-serializable data. Renderers and physics consume it. The generator itself never touches Three.js or Rapier, so it can be unit-tested.

### 3.5 Entities and gameplay (`src/game/*`)
- **Player** (`player/`, T0021): an on-foot state machine (`idle/walk/run/jump/fall/aim/enterVehicle/inVehicle/dead`), health/armour/money, interaction (F to enter or exit the nearest vehicle, which can include carjacking an NPC).
- **Vehicles** (`vehicles/`, T0020): `VehicleDef` data (mass, centre-of-mass offset, engine torque curve, gears, max steer, wheel params and dimensions) for about 6 classes (compact, sports, sedan, van, police, motorbike as a stretch goal). Includes `DriveController` (input or AI produces throttle/brake/steer/handbrake), `VehicleDamage` (health from impulse, smoke at low health, then fire, then explosion) and lights (headlights at night, brake lights).
- **Camera** (`camera/`, T0021 on foot, T0020 in car): a spring-arm follow camera that collides against `WORLD_STATIC` with a shape cast, separate presets for on-foot, in-car (speed-based pull-back and FOV) and aim (over-the-shoulder), plus mouse look with a recenter delay.
- **AI** (`ai/`, a follow-up task): traffic drivers follow lane paths on the RoadGraph with a simple intelligent-driver model for gaps and stop-at-junction rules. Pedestrians walk sidewalk edges, flee from gunfire or collisions, and can be car-jacked or hit. Police (cars and officers) pursue using A* on the RoadGraph plus local steering, ram, and leave the vehicle to chase on foot. A **population manager** keeps N cars and M peds alive in a ring around the player (spawn out of view, despawn far away) with density driven by zone and TimeOfDay.
- **Combat** (`combat/`, follow-up): melee, pistol, SMG and shotgun. Hitscan uses `physics.raycast`, with muzzle flash and tracer from render and synthesised sound from audio.
- **Wanted** (`wanted/`, follow-up): listens to crime events (`vehicleStolen`, `pedHit`, `shotsFired`, `copAttacked`), keeps heat at 0 to 5 stars and decays it while out of police sight. It drives the police spawn tier.
- **Missions** (`missions/`, follow-up): missions are **data**, a list of objective steps (`goTo`, `enterVehicle`, `reachBefore(t)`, `destroy`, `lose wanted`, `deliver`) interpreted by a `MissionRunner`. A start marker sits in the world. The runner shows HUD objective text and a GPS route, and gives pay-out on success. The main story is about 5 to 8 short original missions, enough to "play it once".
- **Save** (`save/`): player position, money, mission progress, time of day, and the city seed (the city is regenerated, not stored).

### 3.6 Input (`src/input/`), owned by T0019 (base) and T0021
- Raw keyboard, mouse (pointer lock) and Gamepad API are mapped to **actions** (`moveX, moveY, lookX, lookY, sprint, jump, enterExit, fire, aim, throttle, brake, steer, handbrake, horn, map, pause`).
- Gameplay reads actions only, never key codes. This makes rebinding and gamepad support free.

### 3.7 Audio (`src/audio/`), follow-up task
- `AudioAPI`: `play(soundId, {position?, volume?, loop?}) → handle`, `setParam(handle, name, value)`, `stop(handle)`, and mixer buses (`sfx, ambience, music, ui`).
- `EngineSynth`: an oscillator and noise model driven by RPM and load per vehicle. `Siren`, `Horn`, `Gunshot`, `Impact`, `Ambience` (waves, city hum, wind).
- "Radio": original procedurally generated synthwave loops (a simple step sequencer). We never use real songs.

### 3.8 UI and HUD (`src/ui/`), owned by T0023
- HUD: health/armour bars, money, wanted stars, weapon/ammo, speedometer in a vehicle, zone name banner, mission objective text and a **minimap** (canvas, player-centred and rotating, drawn from RoadGraph and blips).
- Screens: loading screen with progress from Assets, main menu, pause menu with settings and key bindings, full map, mission passed/failed and "wasted/busted" screens (with original wording).
- The UI is **read-only toward gameplay**. It reads state through a `HudModel` snapshot updated once per frame, and sends user intents back only as events (`ui:resume`, `ui:setting`).

### 3.9 Asset pipeline (`tools/` and `src/assets/`), owned by T0018
- **Two paths:**
  1. **Runtime procedural**: buildings, roads, sidewalks, palms and lamps are generated in the browser from `CityData`. This is cheap to ship and endless in variety.
  2. **Build-time generated glTF**: vehicles, the character mannequin with skeleton and code-authored animation clips (walk, run, idle, enter car), and hero props are generated by Node scripts in `game/tools/` using Three.js and `GLTFExporter`, then compressed (meshopt) into `game/public/assets/*.glb`. Textures (asphalt, concrete, facades) are generated as noise-based canvas textures at runtime or baked to KTX2 by scripts.
- `AssetRegistry`: a typed manifest `assets/manifest.json` mapping `id → {url, type, bytes, lodLevels}`. Code asks for `assets.get('vehicle.sports01')`, never a raw path.
- `AssetLoader`: GLTFLoader, KTX2Loader and MeshoptDecoder with a cache, reference counting (for chunk unload) and a progress callback for the loading screen.
- Conventions (T0018 finalizes them): **1 unit = 1 metre, +Y up, model front faces +Z** (the glTF convention), origin at ground centre for buildings and at the axle midpoint on the ground for vehicles. Wheel nodes are named `wheel_FL/FR/RL/RR`. Ids are lowercase dotted `category.name##`.

### 3.10 Debug and tooling
- F3 overlay: fps, draw calls, triangles, physics ms, entity count, current chunk and seed.
- `?seed=123&spawn=x,z&nopeds` URL flags to make bugs reproducible.
- A `window.__game` handle in dev builds only, so tests and agents can inspect state.

## 4. Module boundaries and rules

### 4.1 Folder layout (T0019 creates it)
```
game/
  package.json  tsconfig.json  vite.config.ts  .eslintrc.cjs  index.html
  public/assets/               # generated .glb/.ktx2 + manifest.json (T0018)
  tools/                       # node scripts: gen-vehicles.ts, gen-character.ts, ...
  src/
    main.ts                    # boot only
    core/      loop.ts ecs/ events.ts services.ts settings.ts time.ts log.ts
    input/     InputAPI.ts keyboardMouse.ts gamepad.ts bindings.ts
    physics/   PhysicsAPI.ts rapier/ (ONLY place importing @dimforge/*)
    render/    RenderAPI.ts renderer.ts scene.ts lighting.ts materials.ts instancing.ts lod.ts water.ts postfx.ts viewSync.ts debugDraw.ts
    audio/     AudioAPI.ts synth/ mixer.ts
    assets/    AssetAPI.ts registry.ts loader.ts procTextures.ts
    ui/        hud/ screens/ minimap.ts hudModel.ts
    game/
      components.ts            # ALL shared component types live here
      events.ts                # ALL event types live here
      world/   cityGen/ roadGraph.ts chunkStreamer.ts zones.ts cityMesher.ts cityColliders.ts
      player/  vehicles/  camera/  ai/  combat/  wanted/  missions/  save/
  tests/       unit/*.test.ts  e2e/smoke.spec.ts
```

### 4.2 Dependency rules (enforced by ESLint `import/no-restricted-paths`)
1. `core/` imports nothing from the project except its own files. Only `three` maths types are allowed.
2. `@dimforge/rapier3d-compat` is imported **only** in `physics/rapier/`. Everyone else uses `PhysicsAPI`.
3. Three.js scene objects (`Mesh`, `Scene`, materials, loaders) are created **only** in `render/`, `assets/`, `game/world/cityMesher.ts` and `*View.ts` files (one view factory per entity type). Gameplay logic files may import only `three` maths classes.
4. `ui/` never imports `game/` modules. It reads `HudModel` and emits events.
5. `game/<a>/` must not import from `game/<b>/` internals. Cross-feature communication uses `game/components.ts`, `game/events.ts` and queries on the ECS world. Shared helpers go in `game/shared/`.
6. Pure generators (`cityGen`, `roadGraph`, mission parsing, wanted logic, AI decision code) have **no** Three.js scene or Rapier dependency, so they are unit-testable in Node.
7. Each module exposes a single `index.ts`. Importing deep paths from another module is a lint error.

### 4.3 Key interfaces (contracts the later tasks implement)
```ts
// core/services.ts
export interface Services {
  physics: PhysicsAPI; render: RenderAPI; audio: AudioAPI; input: InputAPI;
  assets: AssetAPI; events: EventBus<GameEvents>; settings: Settings; time: TimeOfDay;
}
export interface System {
  name: string; phase: Phase;
  init?(world: World, s: Services): void | Promise<void>;
  update(world: World, s: Services, dt: number): void;
  dispose?(): void;
}

// physics/PhysicsAPI.ts
export type BodyHandle = number & { __brand: 'Body' };
export interface PhysicsAPI {
  init(): Promise<void>;                     // loads WASM
  step(dt: number): void;
  createBody(d: BodyDesc): BodyHandle;       // static|dynamic|kinematic + collider shapes + group
  removeBody(h: BodyHandle): void;
  getTransform(h: BodyHandle, out: Transform): Transform;
  setTransform(h: BodyHandle, t: Transform): void;
  applyImpulse(h: BodyHandle, impulse: Vector3, point?: Vector3): void;
  raycast(from: Vector3, dir: Vector3, maxDist: number, mask?: number): RayHit | null;
  shapeCastSphere(from: Vector3, dir: Vector3, radius: number, maxDist: number, mask?: number): RayHit | null;
  createVehicle(d: VehicleDesc): VehicleHandle;      // wraps DynamicRayCastVehicleController
  setVehicleInput(v: VehicleHandle, i: { throttle: number; brake: number; steer: number; handbrake: boolean }): void;
  getVehicleState(v: VehicleHandle): VehicleState;   // speed, rpm-ish, wheel contacts/transforms
  createCharacter(d: CharacterDesc): CharacterHandle; // wraps KinematicCharacterController
  moveCharacter(c: CharacterHandle, desiredDelta: Vector3, dt: number): { grounded: boolean };
  onContact(fn: (e: ContactEvent) => void): () => void;
}

// render/RenderAPI.ts
export interface RenderAPI {
  init(canvas: HTMLCanvasElement): Promise<void>;
  addToWorld(obj: Object3D, layer: 'static' | 'dynamic' | 'debug'): void;
  remove(obj: Object3D): void;
  camera: PerspectiveCamera;
  setTimeOfDay(hours: number): void;
  setQuality(q: 'low' | 'medium' | 'high'): void;
  render(alpha: number): void;
  stats(): { drawCalls: number; triangles: number };
}

// game/world/cityGen/types.ts  (pure data, JSON-serializable)
export interface CityData {
  seed: number; bounds: Rect;
  roadGraph: { nodes: RoadNode[]; edges: RoadEdge[] };   // edges: lanes, width, speedLimit, oneWay
  blocks: Block[]; buildings: Building[];                // footprint polygon, height, style, district
  props: PropPlacement[]; spawnPoints: SpawnPoint[]; zones: Zone[];
}
```

### 4.4 Shared components (`game/components.ts`), first set
`Transform`, `PrevTransform` (for interpolation), `RigidBody {handle}`, `View {object3D}`, `Vehicle {defId, handle, health, occupants[]}`, `Driver {mode: 'player'|'ai'|'none'}`, `Character {handle, state}`, `Health {hp, armor}`, `PlayerTag`, `PedAI {path, state}`, `TrafficAI {laneRoute, targetSpeed}`, `PoliceAI {target, tier}`, `Weapon {id, ammo, cooldown}`, `Blip {icon, color}`, `MissionTarget {missionId, step}`, `Streamed {chunkId}` (despawned together with its chunk).

### 4.5 Events (`game/events.ts`), first set
`collision {a, b, impulse, point}`, `vehicleEntered {entity, vehicle, stolen}`, `vehicleExited`, `damage {target, amount, source, kind}`, `death {entity, cause}`, `shotsFired {pos, weapon}`, `crime {kind, pos, severity}`, `wantedChanged {stars}`, `zoneEntered {zone}`, `missionStarted|Step|Passed|Failed`, `chunkLoaded|Unloaded {chunkId}`, `ui:pause|resume|setting`.

### 4.6 Frame order (one sim tick, then render)
```
input.poll → (actions) → player/AI DriveController & character intent (preSim)
→ physics.step(1/60) → contact events queued (physics)
→ copy body transforms → Transform; Prev saved (postSim)
→ ai (traffic, peds, police) → gameplay (combat, wanted, missions, damage, streaming)
→ events.flush()
render frame: camera system → viewSync(alpha) → render.render(alpha) → ui.update(HudModel)
```

## 5. Performance budget (targets to measure with the F3 overlay)
| Budget | Target (Medium) |
|---|---|
| Frame time | ≤ 16.6 ms total: sim ≤ 6 ms (physics ≤ 3, AI ≤ 2), render submit ≤ 6 ms |
| Draw calls | ≤ 600, reached with instancing, merged static chunk geometry and a shared material library |
| Visible triangles | ≤ 1.5 M |
| Live dynamic actors | about 40 traffic cars, about 60 peds, ≤ 8 police units within the active ring |
| Loaded chunks | 5 × 5 around the player (Low: 3 × 3) |
| Memory | JS heap under 600 MB. Chunk unload must free GPU geometry and physics bodies, and a test checks the counts return to baseline. |

## 6. How the existing tasks map onto this architecture
| Task | Owner (preferred) | Builds | Must respect |
|---|---|---|---|
| T0017 WebGL Engine Research | gpt-1 | Benchmark Three.js / Babylon / PlayCanvas, confirm or overturn §1 | If it recommends switching, only `render/` and `assets/` change. |
| T0018 Asset Pipeline Design | claude-1 | §3.9 in detail: manifest schema, generator scripts, naming | Units, axes and naming in §3.9; glTF/KTX2 |
| T0019 Skeleton Codebase | gpt-1 | `game/` layout §4.1, core loop/ECS/events/services, Rapier init, empty `PhysicsAPI`/`RenderAPI` implementations, lint boundary rules, Vitest and Playwright smoke test, opened as a **PR** | Rules §4.2. Put it in `game/` on a `cate/T0019-*` branch, not a long-lived `browser-gta` branch. |
| T0020 Vehicle Physics | claude-2 | `PhysicsAPI.createVehicle` via Rapier `DynamicRayCastVehicleController`, `VehicleDef`, DriveController, car camera | Rapier only inside `physics/rapier/`. The brief says "Ammo.js or Cannon.js", but **this architecture picks Rapier**, and the supervisor should update that brief. |
| T0021 Character Controller | claude-1 | KinematicCharacterController wrapper, player state machine, on-foot camera, enter/exit vehicle | Read input actions only. |
| T0022 Procedural City | gpt-1 | `generateCity` (pure), RoadGraph, ChunkStreamer, mesher and colliders | `CityData` contract in §4.3 |
| T0023 UI and HUD | gpt-1 | HudModel, DOM HUD, canvas minimap from RoadGraph | UI is read-only toward gameplay. |

**Parts not covered by any task yet (suggested follow-ups for the supervisor to add):**
1. Traffic and pedestrian AI with population manager (§3.5 AI). Depends on T0020, T0021 and T0022.
2. Police and wanted system. Depends on 1.
3. Weapons and combat. Depends on T0021.
4. Procedural audio: engine synth, SFX, ambience, original radio loops (§3.7).
5. Day/night lighting, water, post-FX and quality presets (§3.2).
6. Mission system and 5 to 8 original missions (§3.5 Missions). Depends on most of the above.
7. Save/load, menus, settings.
8. Integration, performance pass and final playtest with a bug list. This is a strict review task covering the "no errors" requirement: zero console errors in a 20-minute session, with the Playwright smoke test in CI.

## 7. Risks and mitigations
| Risk | Mitigation |
|---|---|
| Parallel agents produce code that does not fit together | Typed interfaces in §4.3, a single `components.ts`/`events.ts`, lint-enforced boundaries, and every PR must pass `tsc`, Vitest and the smoke test. |
| Car handling feels bad (the genre's most important feel) | Tunable `VehicleDef` data, a dev panel (lil-gui, dev builds only) for live tuning, and a reviewer drive-test checklist. |
| City too heavy for the browser | Chunk streaming, instancing, LOD, fog distance and the Low preset, measured against §5. |
| Animated humans from scratch are hard | v1 uses a code-generated low-poly mannequin with procedural or code-authored clips. Realism comes from the environment, lighting and vehicles. |
| Rapier vehicle controller docs are thin (the class reference has no usage guide) | T0020 starts from the official class reference and the open-source examples, and writes headless Vitest tests for the controller (car accelerates, stops and turns on flat ground). The `PhysicsAPI` boundary keeps Ammo.js available as a fallback. |
| IP / copying | §0 content rule. Reviewers reject copied names, maps, music or assets. |
| "Perfect, no errors" expectation | Stated honestly: this is a scoped original genre game for one playthrough, not a full commercial-scale replica. Quality is enforced through CI checks and a final integration task. |

## 8. Sources checked for this plan
- Rapier JS `DynamicRayCastVehicleController` class reference (methods include `addWheel`, `setWheelEngineForce`, `setWheelSteering`, `setWheelBrake`, `setWheelSuspensionStiffness`, `setWheelFrictionSlip`, `updateVehicle`, `currentVehicleSpeed`): https://rapier.rs/javascript3d/classes/DynamicRayCastVehicleController.html
- Rapier JS docs root: https://rapier.rs/javascript3d/
- Rapier vehicle documentation gap (issue #90): https://github.com/dimforge/rapier.rs/issues/90
- Three.js releases (r18x series in 2025–2026): https://github.com/mrdoob/three.js/releases
- Three.js WebGPURenderer manual: https://threejs.org/manual/en/webgpurenderer
- Three.js forum, WebGPU renderer performance discussions: https://discourse.threejs.org/tag/webgpu-renderer/1686

**Claims I did not verify:** the exact name of the Rapier factory method (`world.createVehicleController`) was not shown on the class page I fetched; the page documents a constructor taking `(chassis, broadPhase, narrowPhase, bodies, colliders)`. T0020 must check this against the installed package version. I did not confirm Ammo.js's current upstream release status. My reasons for not choosing it (API ergonomics and manual memory management) do not depend on release status. The performance numbers in §5 are design targets, not measurements.

result.text:
# T0017 — WebGL engine research for Neon Coast

Agent: gpt-1. Research date: 2026-11-26.

**Select Three.js with `WebGLRenderer` (WebGL2) for the first playable release.** Keep the TypeScript/Vite, Rapier and rendering boundaries in the approved `data/outputs/T0016.md` architecture. This is a recommendation based on documented capabilities and project fit, not a claim that Three.js is the fastest engine.

The goal is an original, procedurally built coastal-city driving game, playable in a desktop browser. Three.js supplies the rendering pieces without requiring the team to replace the already planned game loop, physics adapter, DOM HUD or entity system. Babylon.js is the strongest alternative if integrated engine tooling becomes more valuable than the existing architecture; PlayCanvas deserves particular consideration if dense dynamic nighttime lighting becomes the dominant requirement.

## Comparison

| Criterion | Three.js | Babylon.js | PlayCanvas Engine |
|---|---|---|---|
| Realistic city visuals | Metallic/roughness PBR through `MeshStandardMaterial`; environment lighting supports convincing roads, buildings and cars. Rendering library: game systems remain our responsibility. | PBR materials plus integrated authoring/debugging tools, including Playground, Inspector and Node Material Editor. Strong option for a team wanting a fuller engine. | PBR and an entity/component engine; clustered lighting is particularly useful for streetlights, headlights and neon-lit streets. |
| Repeated city geometry | `InstancedMesh` reduces draw calls for repeated geometry/materials. Divide batches geographically so their bounds remain useful for visibility checks. | Thin instances reduce per-instance JavaScript object overhead for mostly static repetition. Their all-or-nothing batch visibility and more expensive insertion/removal require deliberate chunking. | Batching reduces draw calls; material/shader reuse helps avoid compilation stalls. Its own component systems require adapting the approved custom architecture. |
| Main performance risks | Too many separate meshes, material variants, real lights and shadow passes; the application must manage streaming and resource lifetimes. | Integrated features still need budgeting. A city-wide thin-instance batch can render much more than is visible; freezing or caching data must respect moving content. | Clustered lighting narrows the lights evaluated per fragment, but CPU cluster updates, overlapping lights and shadow rendering still cost time. It does not make unlimited shadow-casting lights free. |
| Community/support fit | Official examples, API documentation, forum, Discord and linked learning resources support a code-driven workflow. Examples must match the installed release. | Documentation, runnable Playground examples and dedicated questions/bugs/tutorials forum make isolated repros and debugging convenient. | Engine examples, standalone documentation and a forum covering both engine and Editor offer practical support. Distinguish Editor instructions from standalone engine instructions. |
| Runtime license | MIT; compatible with distributing this original browser game, with notices retained. | Apache-2.0; compatible with this use, with its redistribution conditions observed. | MIT for the engine; compatible with this use, with notices retained. The engine can run standalone. |
| Project-fit judgment | **Best fit for the approved modular, code-generated game.** | Best fallback for more integrated development tools. | Strong alternative for clustered lighting or an engine-native component workflow. |

Rendering evidence: [Three.js PBR](https://threejs.org/docs/pages/MeshStandardMaterial.html), [Three.js instancing](https://threejs.org/docs/pages/InstancedMesh.html), [Babylon PBR](https://doc.babylonjs.com/features/featuresDeepDive/materials/using/introToPBR/), [Babylon thin instances](https://doc.babylonjs.com/features/featuresDeepDive/mesh/copies/thinInstances/), [PlayCanvas PBR](https://developer.playcanvas.com/user-manual/graphics/physical-rendering/), [PlayCanvas clustered lighting](https://developer.playcanvas.com/user-manual/graphics/lighting/clustered-lighting/) and [PlayCanvas optimization guidance](https://developer.playcanvas.com/user-manual/optimization/guidelines/).

Support evidence: [Three.js official resource directory](https://threejs.org/), [Babylon tools](https://www.babylonjs.com/), [Babylon forum](https://forum.babylonjs.com/), [PlayCanvas engine documentation](https://developer.playcanvas.com/user-manual/engine/) and [PlayCanvas forum](https://forum.playcanvas.com/). These show available support channels, not guaranteed response times. No community-size ranking or popularity-based performance claim is needed for this decision.

## Performance assessment and implementation guidance

All three provide credible foundations. Actual frame rate depends on scene content, shaders, resolution, shadows, browser, hardware and simulation work. No comparable application benchmark was run for this task, so there are no measured FPS, memory or bundle-size rankings. T0016 says T0017 will benchmark formally; this report completes the assigned documentation-based evaluation but **does not fulfill that additional benchmark expectation**. The following measurement procedure is a proposed implementation gate, not a completed experiment.

For Three.js, begin with these project-specific engineering choices:

1. Batch repeated buildings, palms and street furniture by chunk, geometry and material. Recompute bounds when transforms change; do not use one enormous city-wide instance batch. Keep interactive entities independently addressable in the simulation. Three.js documents both draw-call savings and bounding-volume maintenance for [InstancedMesh](https://threejs.org/docs/pages/InstancedMesh.html).
2. Use metallic/roughness materials and environment lighting for visual coherence. Spend detail on the player car and nearby streets. Start with one shadow-casting sun, limited shadow distance and a small nearby light pool. Use emissive signs/windows for distant nighttime appearance; emissive surfaces alone do not illuminate their surroundings. These are proposed quality/cost choices, not measured optimal settings.
3. Stream city chunks, reduce distant detail, reuse shared materials, release unused GPU resources, and avoid allocating temporary vectors every frame. Budget traffic physics and pedestrian AI separately: changing the renderer cannot fix a simulation bottleneck.
4. Make expensive effects optional. A Low preset should reduce internal resolution, shadow quality/distance, visible world distance and simulation population. Preserve legibility and driving responsiveness before adding reflections or heavy post-processing.
5. Pin the tested engine version and matching addon imports in the lockfile. Check WebGL2 availability and show a useful unsupported-browser message. Current Three.js `WebGLRenderer` requires WebGL2 and has not supported WebGL1 since r163; “WebGL2 runs everywhere” in T0016 is too broad. Keep WebGPU outside the first-release requirement; this report does not verify the earlier architecture's assertion about WebGPU CPU regressions. [WebGLRenderer documentation](https://threejs.org/docs/pages/WebGLRenderer.html).

### Proposed reproducible performance gate

Use a deterministic, representative city scene: repeated opaque buildings and props, moving cars, animated pedestrians, a day route, and a night route with headlights and streetlights. Record object/triangle/material/light counts and all quality settings. Test a production build over HTTP on identified physical hardware; a headless software renderer is not evidence for laptop GPU performance.

For any engine comparison, use identical geometry/textures, camera route, viewport and internal resolution, equivalent shadows/post-effects, the same WebGL2 backend, and either disable simulation in all three or use identical simulation work. Warm up shader compilation, then record three 60-second runs per scene. Report median and p95 frame times, CPU simulation/render submission time, GPU time where supported, draw calls across all passes, compressed transfer bytes, cold-load time, and resource growth across repeated chunk loads/unloads. Document browser, OS, GPU, driver, power mode and exact package versions. Inspect output quality so reduced visual work is not mistaken for a faster engine.

Retain T0016's **targets**, not promises: 60 FPS at 1080p on a defined mid-range laptop (about 16.7 ms/frame), a playable 30 FPS Low preset on defined integrated graphics (about 33.3 ms/frame), and roughly 30 MB or less for first playable transfer. If these fail, profile the actual bottleneck before considering an engine switch. Three.js exposes rendering/resource counters through `renderer.info`; accumulate all passes rather than accidentally reading only the last one. [Renderer monitoring API](https://threejs.org/docs/pages/WebGLRenderer.html).

## Licensing decision

All three core engine licenses permit use and redistribution in the proposed original game. None requires publishing the game's source merely because it uses the engine.

- **Three.js — MIT:** retain its copyright and permission notice in distributed copies/substantial portions. Include the license in the shipped third-party notices. [Upstream license](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/mrdoob/three.js/dev/LICENSE).
- **Babylon.js — Apache-2.0:** distribute the license, retain applicable notices, mark modified upstream files, and reproduce applicable NOTICE attributions if supplied. The license also contains an explicit patent grant and its conditions. [Upstream license](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/BabylonJS/Babylon.js/master/license.md).
- **PlayCanvas Engine — MIT:** retain copyright and permission notices. Standalone engine use does not require adopting the hosted Editor; assess any hosted service separately if introduced. [Engine license](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/playcanvas/engine/main/LICENSE), [standalone engine documentation](https://developer.playcanvas.com/user-manual/engine/).

This confirms compatibility of the engine choices with the intended distribution, not an audit of a future dependency tree. T0019 should preserve notices for the actual pinned dependencies and any decoders; T0018 should track asset provenance. Engine licenses do not grant rights to GTA assets. Keep the original Neon Coast setting and generated assets required by T0016.

## Handoff

T0019 can proceed with Three.js/WebGL2 in `game/` and the approved module contracts. Do not switch the physics stack or add a second renderer for this research decision. T0018 should retain the agreed asset pipeline. Add the representative performance scene during implementation and use measurements to tune quality presets. Reconsider Babylon.js for integrated-tooling needs or PlayCanvas for a demonstrated lighting bottleneck only when the likely gain justifies integration changes.

Research only: no repository code changed, no PR required, and no benchmark or game tests claimed. Primary documentation and license pages cited above were successfully opened for this report.

# Review of T0017 (gpt-1) by claude-2 — PASS, score 85

## What I checked
- Read data/outputs/T0016.md. The quotes the report attributes to it are accurate: the 60 fps / 30 fps Low preset / ~30 MB targets, "T0017 benchmarks them formally", "WebGL2 runs everywhere", and the WebGPU CPU-regression claim.
- Opened the main cited URLs (Three.js WebGLRenderer and InstancedMesh docs, Babylon thin instances, PlayCanvas clustered lighting and standalone-engine docs, all three upstream LICENSE files). All returned HTTP 200. The license files match what the report says: Babylon.js is Apache 2.0, PlayCanvas engine is MIT (Copyright PlayCanvas Ltd), Three.js is MIT.
- The claim that Three.js dropped WebGL1 in r163 matches my own knowledge of the release history.

## Checks
- **Engine selected: PASS.** It clearly picks Three.js with WebGLRenderer (WebGL2). The reasons tie to the approved T0016 architecture, and it names fallbacks with the conditions that would trigger them (Babylon for integrated tooling, PlayCanvas for clustered lighting).
- **Performance notes included: PASS.** It compares each engine's batching approach (InstancedMesh, thin instances, batching), the main performance risks, and clustered lighting costs. It gives concrete, specific guidance for Three.js and a well-designed, reproducible benchmark protocol (median/p95 frame times, all-pass draw calls, warm-up, real hardware).
- **License compatible: PASS.** It gives the correct license for each engine and the obligations that come with it (keeping notices; for Apache-2.0, the NOTICE file, marking modified files, and the patent grant). It correctly says none of them forces the game's source to be published. It also says, correctly, that the engine licenses give no rights to GTA assets.

## Strengths
- Very honest. It says plainly that no benchmark was run, that there are no measured FPS, memory or bundle-size rankings, and that it does not meet T0016's expectation of a formal benchmark. It turns the benchmark into a proposed implementation gate instead.
- It corrects an overbroad claim in T0016 ("WebGL2 runs everywhere") and recommends a fallback message for unsupported browsers.
- It cites primary sources throughout.

## Weaknesses (why the score is not higher)
- The performance comparison is based only on documentation; there is no measured data. The brief says "compare performance", and T0016 expected benchmarks. This is disclosed, and the proposed gate partly makes up for it, but it is still the biggest gap.
- The community-support comparison is qualitative only (it lists channels). It gives no indicators such as release cadence, number of contributors or npm downloads, even though these are easy to check and would make "community support" concrete.
- It does not mention BatchedMesh or LOD for Three.js, which T0016 lists and which matter for city rendering. This is minor.

## Suggested follow-up (optional, non-blocking)
During T0019, implement the proposed performance gate scene, at least for Three.js, so the T0016 targets are measured.

# T0018: Asset pipeline design for Neon Coast

Agent: claude-1. Date: 2026-11-26. Status: design. No game code lands in this task. T0019 creates `game/`, and the generators below are built in the tasks that need them (see §10).

This document expands §3.9 of the approved architecture (`data/outputs/T0016.md`) and stays inside the Three.js/WebGL2 decision confirmed in `data/outputs/T0017.md`. Fixed inputs I did not change: glTF 2.0 binary, meshopt compression, 1 unit = 1 m, +Y up, models face +Z, wheel nodes `wheel_FL/FR/RL/RR`, ids `category.name##`, everything original (the §0 content rule).

**I tested the core of the pipeline before writing this** (§9): a code-built low-poly car went through Three.js `GLTFExporter` in Node 24, then glTF-Transform meshopt compression, then the Khronos glTF validator. The result had 0 errors and 0 warnings, the output was byte-identical across two runs, and the file went from 22,632 to 5,236 bytes. So the toolchain below has been run, not just guessed.

---

## 1. Summary

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| **Asset types** | Buildings, roads and city ground, street furniture, vehicles, the character, weapons, hero/mission props, textures and animation clips (full list in §2) |
| **Generation method** | **A. Runtime procedural:** buildings, roads, sidewalks, palms, lamps and city textures are built in the browser from `CityData` with seeded code. **B. Build-time procedural glTF:** vehicles, the character with its skeleton and clips, weapons and hero props are built by Node scripts from parameter tables with Three.js, then exported. Nothing is modelled by hand and nothing is downloaded. |
| **File format** | **glTF 2.0 binary `.glb`**, geometry compressed with **`EXT_meshopt_compression`** (plus `KHR_mesh_quantization`), loaded by `GLTFLoader` and `MeshoptDecoder`. Textures are procedural `CanvasTexture`s in v1. **KTX2/Basis** is an optional later step (§6.3). Draco is not used. |
| **Storage** | Generator code in `game/tools/assets/`, outputs in `game/public/assets/<category>/<name##>.glb`, and one `game/public/assets/manifest.json` (§7) |
| **Naming** | Lowercase dotted ids, fixed node, material, bone and clip vocabularies, and a lint step that fails the build on violations (§8) |

---

## 2. Asset types

### 2.1 Runtime procedural (generated in the browser, never stored as files)

| Type | Variants for v1 | Built from | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Buildings** | 9 styles: `beach_hotel`, `beach_shop`, `downtown_tower`, `downtown_office`, `res_house`, `res_lowrise`, `ind_warehouse`, plus `air_hangar` and `air_terminal` for the airport | `CityData.buildings` (footprint, height, style, district) | T0022 (mesher), this design (§4) |

## 3. Shared rules for every generator

1. **Units and axes:** 1 unit = 1 m, +Y up, front faces **+Z** (glTF convention), right-handed.
2. **Origins:** buildings sit at the footprint centroid on the ground (y = 0). Vehicles sit at the midpoint between the axles at ground height with the wheels touching y = 0 at rest. The character's origin is between the feet on the ground. Props sit at the bottom centre. Weapons use the grip point.
3. **Determinism:** every generator takes `(params, seed)` and uses one seeded PRNG (`mulberry32`) in `game/src/shared/rng.ts`, shared by tools and runtime. Seeds per item are `hash32(citySeed, chunkX, chunkZ, index)` at runtime and `hash32(assetId)` at build time. `Math.random()` is banned by lint in generators. Same inputs must give byte-identical output (tested, §9).
4. **Materials are a contract, not data:** materials are named from a fixed list (§8.3). At load time `AssetLoader` swaps each named material for the shared instance in `render/materials.ts` (`MaterialLibrary`). Fewer distinct materials means fewer shader programs and better batching (T0016 §5, ≤ 600 draw calls). The colours exported in the `.glb` are fallbacks.
5. **No textures inside `.glb` files in v1:** vehicles, the character, weapons and props use flat PBR values and vertex colours. That keeps files at a few KB and avoids any image codec in Node.
6. **Triangle budgets** (checked by the build, §7.3) are derived from T0016 §5 (≤ 1.5 M visible triangles, about 40 cars, about 60 peds, 5 × 5 chunks):

| Asset | LOD0 | LOD1 | LOD2 |
|---|---|---|---|
| Vehicle | ≤ 3,000 | ≤ 800 | ≤ 150 (box body + 4 wheel boxes) |
| Character | ≤ 2,500 | ≤ 900 | none (culled beyond 120 m) |
| Weapon | ≤ 600 | none | none |
| Hero prop | ≤ 800 | ≤ 200 | none |
| Buildings, per 256 m chunk | ≤ 60,000 | ≤ 12,000 | ≤ 2,000 (skyline slabs) |
| Street furniture instance | ≤ 400 | ≤ 80 | none |

LOD switch distances are 0–60 m, 60–150 m and 150 m to fog for dynamic models, and the T0016 values of 150 m and fog for chunks. `render/lod.ts` owns the numbers. Assets only carry the levels.

## 4. Buildings: runtime procedural method

The code lives in `game/src/assets/procedural/buildings/` and builds `BufferGeometry` only. The scene objects are made by `game/world/cityMesher.ts`, as T0016 §4.2 rule 3 requires. The inputs are pure `Building` records from `CityData`. The output per chunk is **one merged geometry per shared material** plus collider data, so a chunk costs a few draw calls whatever its building count.

**Pipeline per building:**

1. **Footprint cleanup.** Make the polygon counter-clockwise, merge edges shorter than 1.5 m, and snap near-right angles to 90°. If it is not convex, split it into rectangles; `cityGen` should emit rectangles, L shapes and U shapes only.
2. **Floor plan.** Floor heights are set per style: residential 3.0 m, office/tower 3.6 m, hotel 3.2 m, and a ground floor of 4.5 m for shops and hotels. Floors are `max(1, round((height − ground) / floorH)) + 1`. The final height is then recomputed, so window rows always line up.
3. **Massing (style grammar).**
   - `downtown_tower`: a podium of 2–3 floors at the full footprint. The tower above is inset 2–4 m, with 0–2 setbacks (another 2–3 m inset every 8–15 floors, chosen by the seed). It has a crown: a flat roof, a stepped roof or a helipad box.
   - `beach_hotel`: a slab with balcony strips facing the sea side (the edge closest to the coastline from `zones`), a ground-floor colonnade, rounded corners (each corner chamfered into 3 segments, which reads as the period's streamline style) and a rooftop sign frame.
   - `beach_shop`: 1–2 floors with an awning box over the shopfront and a neon sign plane.
   - `res_house`: 1–2 floors with a hip roof or a flat roof with parapet, set back from the plot edge.
   - `res_lowrise`: 3–6 floors with external walkway boxes on one side.
   - `ind_warehouse` and `air_hangar`: a single tall volume with a shallow gable or barrel roof (8-segment arc) and roller-door insets.
   - `air_terminal`: a long low box with a glass curtain wall material.
4. **Facades.** Each footprint edge is split into **bays** about 3 m wide (`bays = max(1, round(edgeLen / 3))`). Each floor × bay is one quad with UVs into that style's **facade atlas** (§6). The atlas has cells for wall-only, window, double window, door, shopfront, balcony window and blank. The seed picks a per-building pattern (for example every bay windowed, or alternating), and a per-building tint goes into a vertex colour, so one material covers a whole district with visible variety. Windows are **texture, not geometry**, which is what keeps LOD0 inside budget.
5. **Night lighting.** The atlas has an emissive mask for windows. A per-vertex `aLit` value (0/1, seeded about 35% lit) multiplies it, so windows switch on at dusk through one material uniform driven by `TimeOfDay`, with no per-building work.
6. **Roof.** A flat cap with a 0.6 m parapet. Roof clutter (AC units, water tanks, antennas, stair boxes) is placed by the seed and rendered as `InstancedMesh` per chunk, not merged.
7. **LOD0 details** (only within 150 m): balcony slabs, awnings, colonnade pillars and sign planes, all simple boxes merged into the chunk geometry.
8. **Merge per chunk.** Call `BufferGeometryUtils.mergeGeometries()` (Three.js addon, present in r187) once per material. Keep a `buildingId → [indexStart, indexCount]` table so debug tools can highlight a building.
9. **LOD1.** The same footprint extruded once (walls and roof, no details) with the same atlas UVs, so windows still read from a distance. This is generated in the same pass.
10. **LOD2.** One box per building merged into a "skyline" mesh with a cheap material, used beyond 150 m up to the fog distance.
11. **Colliders (data only, for `cityColliders.ts`).** Use one oriented box per footprint rectangle, `{center, halfExtents, rotationY}`, at full height. Setbacks add one box per tier. Trimesh colliders are not used for buildings because boxes are cheaper in Rapier and good enough for cars and the camera.
12. **Disposal.** The chunk owner keeps references to every geometry it created and disposes them when the chunk unloads. The memory baseline test in T0016 §5 covers this.

**Roads, sidewalks and ground** follow the same pattern: ribbons extruded along `RoadEdge` polylines with lane-marking UVs, junction polygons from node fans, and kerb strips 0.15 m high. Each is merged per chunk per material. T0022 owns the exact algorithm; this design fixes only the material names (§8.3) and the UV scale (1 UV unit = 4 m on asphalt).

**Street furniture** geometry is built once at boot by small functions in `src/assets/procedural/props/` (for example, a palm is a tapered 6-sided trunk with 8 curved frond strips and seeded lean), then drawn with one `InstancedMesh` per prop type per chunk (T0017 rule: batch by chunk, not city-wide).

## 5. Vehicles, character, weapons and props: build-time glTF method

### 5.1 Toolchain (versions checked on npm on 2026-11-26)

| Tool | Version | Use |
|---|---|---|
| Node | 24 LTS (tested on 24.22.3) | Runs the scripts with `node --experimental-strip-types` or `tsx` (T0019's choice) |
| `three` | 0.187.0 | Builds the meshes, plus `GLTFExporter` (`three/addons/exporters/GLTFExporter.js`) |
| `@gltf-transform/core`, `/functions`, `/extensions` | 4.5.1 | Post-processing: `dedup`, `weld`, `prune`, `meshopt` |
| `meshoptimizer` | 1.3.0 | Encoder for `EXT_meshopt_compression` |
| `gltf-validator` | npm package (reports validator 2.0.0-dev.3.10) | Spec validation in the build and in tests |

All of these are **dev dependencies**. At runtime the game needs only `three` (with its bundled `meshopt_decoder.module.js`), which T0016 already lists.

**One known Node gap, handled:** `GLTFExporter` with `binary: true` uses `FileReader`, which Node 24 does not provide (`typeof FileReader === 'undefined'`; I checked). The pipeline installs a 6-line `FileReader` shim built on `Blob.arrayBuffer()` (`tools/assets/lib/nodeShims.ts`, shown in §9). Since no textures go into the `.glb` files, no canvas or image encoding is needed in Node. **Fallback:** if the shim ever breaks after a Three.js upgrade, the generators can write geometry straight into a glTF-Transform `Document`, which is Node-native. This costs more code but has no browser APIs.

### 5.2 Vehicles (`tools/assets/gen/vehicles.ts`)

Each vehicle is a **parameter row**, not a model:

```ts
interface VehicleShape {
  id: `vehicle.${string}`;            // 'vehicle.sedan01'
  length: number; width: number; height: number;   // metres
  wheelbase: number; track: number; wheelRadius: number; wheelWidth: number;
  groundClearance: number;
  profile: Array<[z: number, y: number]>;  // side silhouette, front (+Z) to back, 10–16 points
  cabin: { zFront: number; zBack: number; roofY: number; taper: number };  // glass house
  bumpers: boolean; spoiler?: boolean; roofSign?: 'taxi' | 'siren';
  paint: 'tintable' | string;         // police/taxi use fixed palette ids
}
```

**Method:**
1. **Body.** Extrude the side `profile` across the width with a small bevel (`ExtrudeGeometry`, `bevelSegments: 1`). Then pinch the top edge inward by `taper` so it is not a slab. The result is about 300–900 triangles.
2. **Glass house.** A second extruded profile between `cabin.zFront` and `cabin.zBack`, inset 5 cm, using `mat_glass`.
3. **Wheel arches.** Cut by boolean-free means: the profile polyline gets an arc notch at each axle, so no CSG library is needed.
4. **Wheels.** One cylinder (16 sides at LOD0, 8 at LOD1) plus a rim disc, as **separate nodes** `wheel_FL/FR/RL/RR`. Each wheel's origin is the wheel centre, so the physics transform can drive it directly.
5. **Lights.** Small emissive boxes in their own nodes (`light_head_L/R`, `light_brake_L/R`, plus `light_siren_L/R` for police) so the light system can toggle them or swap the emissive strength.
6. **Sockets.** Empty nodes for gameplay: `socket_seat_driver`, `socket_door_L`, `socket_door_R` (where a character stands to enter), `socket_exhaust` (smoke and backfire), `socket_engine` (fire and smoke at low health) and `socket_camera` (in-car camera target).
7. **LODs.** The same function is called with lower segment counts (and LOD2 as boxes), producing three child groups `lod0/lod1/lod2` under the root. Wheels and sockets sit directly under the root and are shared by all levels. LOD2 hides the wheel meshes.
8. **Paint variation.** The body uses `mat_paint`. At spawn, the runtime picks from an 8-colour 1980s-coast palette and gets one cached material clone per colour, so a full traffic load has at most 8 paint materials.
9. **Physics hand-off.** The generator writes the true wheel centres, radius, chassis half-extents and centre of mass into the manifest `meta` (§7). T0020's `VehicleDef` **reads these instead of re-typing numbers**, so the visual wheels and the raycast wheels cannot drift apart.

### 5.3 Character (`tools/assets/gen/character.ts`)

1. **Skeleton.** 19 bones (`root, hips, spine, chest, neck, head`, and `_L/_R` versions of `shoulder, upperarm, forearm, hand, thigh, shin, foot`). The mannequin is 1.80 m tall, facing +Z.
2. **Mesh.** Each body part is a low-poly capsule or box (6–8 sides), rigidly skinned to one bone (weight 1.0). Joint rings at the elbows, knees and hips are blended 50/50 to their two bones so bends do not tear. One `SkinnedMesh`, ≤ 2,500 triangles. Materials `mat_skin`, `mat_cloth_top`, `mat_cloth_bottom`, `mat_shoe`, all tintable for crowd variety.
3. **Clips.** Each clip is written as a keyframe table in code: about 4–8 keys per bone of quaternions per clip, sampled from simple periodic functions (for example, a walk cycle is thigh swing = A·sin(2πt/T), with knee bend phase-shifted). Each table is turned into `THREE.AnimationClip` objects and passed to the exporter's `animations` option. Root motion is **not** baked; the controller moves the capsule (T0021).
4. **Sockets.** `socket_hand_R` (weapon grip), `socket_head` (hats/hair blocks), plus a `socket_seat` offset so the sitting pose lines up with `socket_seat_driver`.
5. **Runtime cloning** uses `SkeletonUtils.clone()` (Three.js addon, present in r187) so each ped gets its own skeleton.

### 5.4 Weapons and hero props (`gen/weapons.ts`, `gen/props.ts`)

Boxes, cylinders and simple extrusions only. Weapons carry `socket_grip` (the origin) and `socket_muzzle`. Props carry a `collider` record in the manifest (`box` half-extents or `cylinder` radius and height) and a `mass` for dynamic ones (cone 3 kg, barrier 20 kg, crate 25 kg, dumpster static). Pickups use `mat_pickup_*` emissive materials and spin at runtime.

### 5.5 Build steps (`npm run assets` → `tools/assets/build.ts`)

```
for each definition (vehicles, character, weapons, props):
  1. generate   Object3D tree from (params, seed)              [gen/*.ts]
  2. lint       names, origin, axes, sockets, LOD groups,
                triangle budget per LOD                        [lib/checks.ts]   → fail build on error
  3. export     GLTFExporter.parseAsync(scene, {binary:true,
                animations})                                   [lib/exportGlb.ts]
  4. optimise   glTF-Transform: dedup → weld → prune → meshopt [lib/optimize.ts]
  5. validate   gltf-validator: numErrors must be 0            [lib/validate.ts]
  6. write      public/assets/<category>/<name##>.glb
  7. record     bytes, sha256, triangles per LOD, bounds,
                meta, provenance                               → manifest entry
write public/assets/manifest.json (keys sorted, 2-space JSON, stable)
```

- `npm run assets` regenerates everything. Run time for the full set has not been measured yet.
- `npm run assets:check` regenerates to a temp directory and fails if any hash differs from the committed manifest. A Vitest test (`tests/unit/assets.test.ts`) calls the same check, so the existing `npm test` covers it. **No workflow change is needed**, which matters because agents cannot edit `.github/workflows/`.
- **The generated `.glb` files and `manifest.json` are committed.** They are small (about 5 KB per car measured; the full set should be well under 1 MB, an estimate to confirm), and committing them means `npm run dev` and the static deploy work without running generators. It also means a reviewer can see in the manifest diff exactly which assets changed. The determinism check stops hand edits or stale files.

## 6. Textures

### 6.1 v1: procedural canvas textures at runtime (`src/assets/procTextures.ts`)

They are generated once at boot on an `OffscreenCanvas` (or a `<canvas>` as fallback) with seeded value noise plus drawing calls, then wrapped in `THREE.CanvasTexture` with mipmaps and repeat wrapping:

| Texture | Size | Content |
|---|---|---|
| `tex_asphalt_basecolor` | 1024² | Grey noise with sparse aggregate speckles and darker patch stains |
| `tex_asphalt_markings` | 512 × 64 strip | White and yellow lane lines, dashes, stop bar, sampled by road UVs |
| `tex_sidewalk_basecolor` | 512² | Concrete slabs with joint lines |
| `tex_sand_basecolor`, `tex_grass_basecolor` | 512² | Two-octave noise |
| `tex_facade_<style>_basecolor` | 1024² atlas, 4 × 4 cells | Wall, window and door cells for that style, period pastel palettes |
| `tex_facade_<style>_emissive` | 1024² (same layout) | Window glow mask for night |
| `tex_sign_<n>_basecolor` | 512 × 128 | Neon sign faces with **invented** business names from a word list in code |

Normal maps are generated from the same height noise (Sobel filter) for asphalt, sidewalk and facades at the Medium preset and up. Boot cost has to be measured in T0022. If it is above about 300 ms, move to §6.3.

### 6.2 Why not ship image files in v1

Procedural textures add 0 bytes to the download (T0016 size target < 30 MB), need no image codec in Node, and keep every texture provably original.

### 6.3 Later option: KTX2/Basis bake

If GPU memory or boot time is too high, a `tools/assets/gen/textures.ts` step renders the same canvas code in Node or a headless browser to PNG, then runs `gltf-transform etc1s` (colour) or `uastc` (normal maps). **I checked that the glTF-Transform 4.5.1 CLI calls the external `ktx` command from KTX-Software and requires version 4.4.0 or newer.** That is a native binary on the build machine, which is why it is not in v1. If adopted, the runtime adds `KTX2Loader` (with `detectSupport(renderer)`) and the Basis transcoder from `three/examples/jsm/libs/basis/`, both present in r187.

### 6.4 Draco

Draco is not used. Meshopt also compresses animation, decodes faster, and ships as a small decoder inside Three.js. One codec keeps the loader simple.

### 7.3 Runtime loader (`src/assets/loader.ts`) contract

- One `GLTFLoader` with `setMeshoptDecoder(MeshoptDecoder)` from `three/addons/libs/meshopt_decoder.module.js` (both confirmed present in three 0.187.0). `setKTX2Loader` is only needed if §6.3 lands.
- `preload(ids, onProgress)` for the loading screen, using manifest `bytes` as the progress weight.
- A cache keyed by id, with **reference counting**: `acquire(id) → handle`, `release(handle)`. When the count reaches zero, geometries are disposed (chunk unload, T0016 §5 memory test).
- `instantiate(id)` returns a clone. Geometry is shared; skinned assets go through `SkeletonUtils.clone`. Named materials are swapped for `MaterialLibrary` instances (§3 rule 4).
- glTF `extras` come through as `userData`. The spike showed that `GLTFExporter` writes `Object3D.userData` to node `extras` and that it survives meshopt optimisation, so the root node also carries `{assetId, generator, seed}` for debugging.

### 7.4 Provenance

`game/ASSETS.md` states that every asset is generated by code in this repository, lists the generators, and says that **no external meshes, textures, fonts or sounds are used**. Any future external file must be CC0 or similarly licensed, listed there with its source URL and licence, and given `license` other than `original` in the manifest. Reviewers fail a PR that adds a binary asset not produced by `npm run assets`. This covers T0017's request that T0018 track asset provenance, and T0016's §0 content rule.

## 8. Naming conventions

### 8.1 Ids and files
- **Asset id:** `^(vehicle|character|weapon|prop|texture)\.[a-z][a-z0-9_]*[0-9]{2}$`, for example `vehicle.sports01` or `prop.pickup_cash01`. The two-digit suffix allows variants (`vehicle.sedan02`).
- **File:** `public/assets/<category>/<name##>.<glb|ktx2>`, derived from the id and never typed by hand.
- **Runtime procedural keys** (not in the manifest): building styles `<district>_<style>` as in §2.1, building instance `b_<chunkX>_<chunkZ>_<index>`, chunk `c_<x>_<z>`, prop types as lowercase snake names (`traffic_light`).

### 8.2 Nodes inside `.glb` files
| Pattern | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| root = asset id | One root node per file | `vehicle.sedan01` |
| `lod0`, `lod1`, `lod2` | LOD groups under the root | |
| plain lowercase | Mesh parts | `body`, `glass`, `bumper_F` |
| `wheel_FL/FR/RL/RR` | Wheels (T0016), origin at the wheel centre | |
| `light_<kind>_<L/R>` | Light meshes | `light_head_L`, `light_brake_R`, `light_siren_L` |
| `socket_<name>` | Empty attachment points | `socket_seat_driver`, `socket_hand_R`, `socket_muzzle` |
| `_L/_R/_F/_B` suffix | Left/right/front/back from the model's own view (front = +Z, left = +X when facing +Z) | |

### 8.3 Materials (fixed list, `mat_` prefix)
Vehicles: `mat_paint`, `mat_glass`, `mat_tire`, `mat_rim`, `mat_chrome`, `mat_plastic_black`, `mat_light_head`, `mat_light_brake`, `mat_light_siren_red`, `mat_light_siren_blue`, `mat_sign_taxi`.

Adding a material means adding it to `MaterialLibrary` and to this list in the same PR.

### 8.4 Bones and clips
Bones are lowercase with `_L/_R` (§5.3). Clips are lowercase snake case with an optional side: `idle`, `walk`, `run`, `jump`, `fall`, `enter_car_L`, `exit_car_L`, `aim_pistol`, `death`.

### 8.5 Textures
`tex_<subject>_<map>` with map ∈ {`basecolor`, `normal`, `orm`, `emissive`, `markings`}, for example `tex_facade_beach_hotel_emissive`.

   ```js
   globalThis.FileReader = class {
     readAsArrayBuffer(b) { b.arrayBuffer().then(r => { this.result = r; this.onloadend?.(); }); }
     readAsDataURL(b) { b.arrayBuffer().then(r => { this.result = `data:${b.type || 'application/octet-stream'};base64,` + Buffer.from(r).toString('base64'); this.onloadend?.(); }); }
   };
   ```

2. **Optimise.** `NodeIO` with `ALL_EXTENSIONS` and the meshopt encoder/decoder registered, then `dedup(), weld(), prune(), meshopt({encoder: MeshoptEncoder, level: 'medium'})`. Result: **5,236 bytes**, using extensions `EXT_meshopt_compression` and `KHR_mesh_quantization`. Node names, material names and root `extras` all survived.

**Not tested here:** skinned mesh and animation export, the full set of generators, runtime loading in a browser, procedural texture boot time, and building-mesher performance. These belong to the implementation tasks, and the checks in §5.5 and §7 are designed to catch problems there.

# T0020: Vehicle physics — done

**Pull request: https://github.com/shloki-loki/CATE/pull/8** (branch `cate/T0020-vehicle-physics`, targets `main`; the owner reviews and merges)

The game is now drivable in the browser. You start in a sports car on the avenue, with four parked cars and the crates at the crossing to drive through or crash into. Controls: W/S throttle and brake (hold S at a standstill to reverse), A/D steer, Space handbrake, R to put the car back on its wheels, mouse drag to look, F3 for the overlay.

**Physics engine:** the brief said "Ammo.js or Cannon.js". The approved architecture (T0016) picked **Rapier**, and the merged skeleton (T0019, PR #6) already runs on it. So I used Rapier's `DynamicRayCastVehicleController`, the same raycast-vehicle model as Ammo.js's `btRaycastVehicle`. Adding a second physics engine to the same world would not work well.

## Evidence for each check
- **Vehicle responds to input:**
  - Headless tests: the car stays still with no input; drives forward on throttle; steers right and left the correct way; brakes from 100 km/h in 30–55 m (measured 38–53 m) and then reverses; R rights an upside-down car.
  - In the real browser build (Playwright, headless Chromium): holding W takes it above 25 km/h, D turns it right, and S stops it. No console errors.
- **Collision detection works:**
  - A wall hit stops the car at the wall face (under 5 cm penetration), sends a `collision` event (other side `null` = static world) with a contact point, and applies damage.
  - At 216 km/h the car does not pass through a 20 cm wall (continuous collision detection is on).
  - Car into a parked car: both cars get the event and damage, and the parked car is shoved.
  - Pushing against a wall sends no events and does no damage. A wrecked car emits `death` and loses drive.
  - In the browser run, the car really hit a parked sedan (health 1000 → 802).
- **Physics stable:**
  - 30 s at rest: under 1 mm of movement per tick.
  - Full-lock cornering at 100 km/h rolls none of the 5 classes over.
  - A ramp jump of about 5 m plus kerbs lands upright.
  - 2 minutes of random driving with 5 cars among walls: no NaN, nothing falls through the ground, no runaway speed.

Test totals:
- `npm run check`: typecheck, lint and build pass; 54/54 unit tests (28 of them new).
- `npm run test:e2e`: 2/2 pass.
- Repo Python tests: 32 OK.

Measured handling (headless, 60 Hz, flat ground):

| class | 0–100 km/h | top speed | 100–0 km/h | steady cornering |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| compact | 9.2 s | 187 km/h | 43.2 m | 0.94 g |
| sedan | 7.8 s | 211 km/h | 43.0 m | 0.90 g |
| sports | 3.9 s | 288 km/h | 37.8 m | 1.10 g |
| van | 11.9 s | 167 km/h | 53.1 m | 0.81 g |
| police | 5.8 s | 239 km/h | 41.9 m | 0.97 g |

## Limits
- There is still **no CI job for `game/`**: agents cannot edit `.github/workflows/`. Everything above was run locally in this job.
- Not done here:
  - Wheels have no simulated spin of their own, so there is no wheelspin or ABS.
  - Rapier's side-friction stiffness barely changes steady cornering. It is the friction-slip (`grip`) value that sets cornering, so the handbrake slide comes mainly from the locked rear.
  - Damage is health only: no smoke, fire or deformation, and no engine sound.
  - No lil-gui tuning panel, no headlights at night, no on-foot enter/exit (T0021).
- Speeds and grip are tuned against typical real-car figures. I have not checked the feel on a real GPU or with a human driver; SwiftShader ran at about 6–34 fps.
- The car models are placeholder boxes (T0018 will replace them). Paint is non-metallic until there is an environment map.

- **Player** (`src/game/player/`):

  - A placeholder mannequin with a procedural walk/run cycle.
- **Follow camera** (`src/game/camera/followCamera.ts`):
  - Spring arm behind the player, following the interpolated position with light smoothing.
  - Mouse look (click to capture the mouse, or drag) and wheel zoom.
  - A sphere sweep against buildings and ground pulls the camera in at once when something is in the way, so it never goes inside walls. When the player is in a car it follows the car.
